task: Write one sentence of your own using the word staid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know staid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Their staid holiday card—cream stock, engraved names, no photo—hasn't changed since 1989.
Sensible is milder than staid—sensible shoes are practical but might still come in red, while a staid wardrobe quietly gave up on red years ago.
Severe goes further than sensible—a severe gray suit strips away every ornament on purpose, while staid merely declines to chase fashion.

Sedate is about pace: a sedate walk, a sedate tempo, nothing hurried. Staid is about style and manner—settled, buttoned-down, allergic to flash. A parade can move at a sedate pace and still be gaudy; a staid firm may work frantically and never show a flourish.

Sober here means serious and plain, with playfulness deliberately set aside—a sober speech, a sober report, dressed for the occasion. Staid goes further in time: seriousness settled into permanent habit, a style that stopped surprising anyone years ago. Sober can be chosen for a day; staid is simply what the place is.

Ask anyone in town about the diner and they will tell you it has been the mainstay of the square since 1962.
Staid means sedate, serious, self-restrained.
The quiz show's new host inherited a staid format—two podiums, a bell, polite applause—and changed nothing but his tie, trusting the show's quiet dignity to keep its loyal audience.
Staid describes a settled, buttoned-down seriousness of style or manner—reliable, a little formal, allergic to flash.
It often carries a faint sigh: staid institutions are trusted, but nobody calls them exciting.
Staid is for styles, institutions, and manners that have settled and stopped surprising anyone—usually with a wry edge, half compliment and half yawn.
Stolid, its unit-mate, is about the face rather than the style: a stolid juror shows no feeling; a staid firm shows no flair.
For pace rather than style, sedate (a chip above) is the closer fit.

For a century the Halbrook Museum was the definition of staid: oak cases, brass plaques, and typed labels in the same narrow font the founder approved.
Then a new director arrived with video walls, a neon lobby installation, and a request that guards wear sneakers.
Longtime members split at once: half canceled their memberships, and half admitted they had not visited in years anyway.

The local paper ran dueling letters for a month, one calling the museum 'a bank lobby with dinosaurs,' another mourning 'the last unhurried room in the city.' The director's compromise is on view now: the neon stays in the lobby, but past the marble arch the old hush and the narrow font remain, kept that way by design.
